title: A solution of bounded dynamic range yields a linearly ordered colouring with logarithmically many colours
source_title: A logarithmic approximation of linearly ordered colourings

proof_spans.label: the complete author proof of the labelled lemma, retained line for line

standard_prerequisites.name: Homogeneous linear system over the reals
standard_prerequisites.statement: The coordinates of a solution are real numbers, with M the largest absolute value and m the smallest positive absolute value.
standard_prerequisites.use: Their ratio controls the number of colours.

standard_prerequisites.name: Linearly ordered colouring
standard_prerequisites.statement: A colouring in which the smallest colour appearing once in an edge is unique.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is what the construction produces.

standard_prerequisites.name: Logarithmic colour classes
standard_prerequisites.statement: The colours are assigned by comparing the absolute value of a coordinate against powers of two, with even colours used for positive coordinates and odd ones for negative coordinates.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the construction whose correctness has to be checked.

core_obligations: Normalise the solution so that the largest absolute value is one and reduce to the requirement that the minimum colour in each edge be unique, since the order of the colours can be reversed at the end (source lines 273-275).
Assign to each vertex the colour determined by the dyadic interval containing its coordinate, using even colours for positive coordinates and odd colours for negative ones (source lines 276-281).

Verify the uniqueness of the minimal colour in every edge, which is where the ratio of the largest to the smallest absolute value enters the count of two plus the logarithm to base two of that ratio (source lines 282-288).

proof_roadmap.step: Normalise and restate the requirement on the minimal colour.
Assign colours by dyadic intervals, positive and negative separately.
Verify uniqueness of the minimal colour in every edge.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 266-271: if a homogeneous system has a solution whose largest absolute coordinate value is M and whose smallest positive absolute value is m, then the associated hypergraph has a linearly ordered colouring with two plus the logarithm to base two of the ratio of M to m colours. The proof (source lines 273-288) changes the shape of the requirement first, asking that the minimum colour in each edge be unique and reversing the colour order at the end, which is only legitimate because the reversal preserves the property; it then assigns colours according to which dyadic interval a coordinate falls into, separately for positive and negative coordinates, and the verification of uniqueness is where the ratio of the extreme absolute values is converted into the number of colours. The statement records the colour count and none of the normalisation or the construction.
